comments.author: participant1
comments.body:
In a causal cluster, per database there is only one leader node that processes write transactions. Followers cannot process writes.

That said, it sounds like you may be interested in server-side routing. When configured for server-side routing only, the client will no longer perform routing, allowing you to issue write transactions to any node in the cluster, but internal to the cluster write transactions will be routed to the leader for processing.

https://neo4j.com/docs/operations-manual/current/clustering/setup/routing/#clustering-routing

comments.author: participant1
comments.body:
You're not using the `neo4j://` routing protocol, however. Your screenshot shows you are using the `bolt://` protocol, which does not engage routing (ANY routing, including server side) and that's likely why you are getting that error. Try with the `neo4j://` protocol instead.

Also, routing is not binary, there are 3 forms it can take depending on the values of two configuration properties: only client-side routing, hybrid client and server side routing (what you likely have configured now), and only server-side routing. 

The two properties governing the routing are:

dbms.routing.enabled - set to a boolean value. If true then enables server-side routing
dbms.routing.default_router - set to either SERVER or CLIENT (CLIENT is default)

So if you have  `dbms.routing.default_router=CLIENT` or are using defaults, and `dbms.routing.enabled=true` then you are using a hybrid routing, where (provided that you are using the `neo4j://` protocol and not the `bolt://` protocol) the driver will still perform the routing, and if the server you routed a write query to is no longer the leader, the server-side routing will route it to the new leader for execution. If `dbms.routing.default_router=CLIENT` and `dbms.routing.enabled=false`, then you are purely using client-side routing. If `dbms.routing.default_router=SERVER` and `dbms.routing.enabled=true`, then you are purely using server-side routing.

Again, for any routing to take place you need to be using the `neo4j://` protocol in the connection address.

comments.author: participant3
comments.body: Hi @participant1, you mentioned "per database there is only one leader node that processes write transactions.", but I noticed that many docs said that there may be multi "core server" in a cluster, does leader and follower node together called "core server". or only leader node called "core server", is it possible there are many leader in a cluster?

comments.author: participant1
comments.body:
@participant3 One common issue with tech is that there are terms which are overloaded.

I'm fairly sure "multi core server" uses "core" to mean "cpu core", which has only to do with hardware components, and nothing to do with Neo4j and clustering.

When we're talking about Neo4j and clustering, "core" is referring to a Neo4j process running on a single server that is configured as `dbms.mode=CORE` (using 4.x config and terminology; there have been changes in 5.x) meaning that in a causal cluster it participates in the Raft protocol, and may be elected a leader for some subset of databases (and if not a db leader, then a follower).

It's also important to remember that Neo4j (as a dbms and cluster) supports multiple databases, and leadership can be different per database.

So if you had a 3 core cluster and 3 databases on your dbms: system, northwind, movies
then it's possible that core 1 could be the `movies` db leader, core 2 could be the `system` db leader, and core 3 could be the `northwind` db leader (with all other nodes otherwise being followers for the databases where they do not hold leadership). When there are more databases than there are cores in the cluster, then some cores may be leaders for multiple databases.

With that in mind, when we're talking about routing to the leader, it is the leader for the database you've specified when you create the transaction or session.

comments.author: participant1
comments.body:
> I think this is just client-side route, not server-side route.

Yes, it likely is, since you've enabled server-side routing, but you have not disabled client-side routing, both of them can coexist, with server-side routing being used only when client-side routing routes to the wrong server (such as a timing issue during a leader switch). 

Have you applied `dbms.routing.default_router=SERVER` yet? That should disable client-side routing, and allow server-side routing to be the only routing system being used.

comments.author: participant1
comments.body:
For ONLY server-side routing you need these:

```
dbms.routing.default_router=SERVER
dbms.routing.enabled=true
```

At that point as long as you are using the `neo4j://` protocol in the connection address, you can connect to any node (or any address that resolves to any node in the cluster, or use a load balancer) and the node will accept the transaction and route it to the leader internally (if it's a write) or execute it immediately if it's a read.
